# Matrix Spaces and Rank

- [A matrix has four fundamental subspaces](#a-matrix-has-four-fundamental-subspaces)
- [Rank and nullity measure different parts of a matrix](#rank-and-nullity-measure-different-parts-of-a-matrix)
- [One reduction exposes the structure](#one-reduction-exposes-the-structure)
- [Column and row bases come from different matrices](#column-and-row-bases-come-from-different-matrices)
- [Free variables build a basis for the null space](#free-variables-build-a-basis-for-the-null-space)

## A matrix has four fundamental subspaces {#a-matrix-has-four-fundamental-subspaces}

For an $m\times n$ matrix $\mat{A}$:

| Space | Definition | Lives in |
|---|---|---|
| $\operatorname{Col}(\mat{A})$ | span of the columns of $\mat{A}$ | $\reals^m$ |
| $\operatorname{Null}(\mat{A})$ | solutions of $\mat{A}\vct{x}=\vct{0}$ | $\reals^n$ |
| $\operatorname{Row}(\mat{A})$ | span of the rows of $\mat{A}$ | $\reals^n$ |
| $\operatorname{Null}(\mat{A}^{\mathsf T})$ | solutions of $\mat{A}^{\mathsf T}\vct{y}=\vct{0}$ | $\reals^m$ |

::: {.key-point}
Always identify the ambient space before comparing subspaces

View row-space vectors as columns by transposing the matrix rows
:::

## Rank and nullity measure different parts of a matrix {#rank-and-nullity-measure-different-parts-of-a-matrix}

Recall: [dimension]({{< meta decks.d06b.file >}}#dimension-counts-vectors-in-any-basis) is the number of vectors in a basis

For $\mat{A}\in\reals^{m\times n}$, define

$$
\operatorname{rank}(\mat{A})=\dim(\operatorname{Col}(\mat{A})),
\qquad
\operatorname{nullity}(\mat{A})=\dim(\operatorname{Null}(\mat{A}))
$$

Row reduction gives

- rank = number of pivot columns = dimension of the row space
- nullity = number of free variables

$$
0\le\operatorname{rank}(\mat{A})\le\min(m,n)
$$

::: {.key-point}
Rank counts independent output directions; nullity counts lost input directions
:::

::: {.notes}
Rank is defined here using column-space dimension. The row-rank/column-rank
theorem says the dimensions agree. Pivot columns of the original matrix are
a column-space basis; the nonzero [RREF]({{< meta decks.d01.file >}}#reduced-row-echelon-form)
rows are a row-space basis with the
same number of vectors. Each free variable contributes one independent
null-space vector. We use real matrices throughout this deck.
:::

## One reduction exposes the structure {#one-reduction-exposes-the-structure}

Use one example throughout, recalling
[pivots and free variables from {{< meta decks.d01.short_title >}}]({{< meta decks.d01.file >}}#eliminate-and-organize-with-pivots):

$$
\mat{A}=
\begin{bmatrix}
1&2&1&3\\
2&4&0&4\\
1&2&2&4
\end{bmatrix}
\quad\longrightarrow\quad
\operatorname{rref}(\mat{A})=
\left[
\begin{array}{cccc}
\bbox[3px,border:2px solid teal]{\begin{matrix}1\\0\\0\end{matrix}}
&\begin{matrix}2\\0\\0\end{matrix}
&\bbox[3px,border:2px solid teal]{\begin{matrix}0\\1\\0\end{matrix}}
&\begin{matrix}2\\1\\0\end{matrix}
\end{array}
\right]
$$

The [RREF]({{< meta decks.d01.file >}}#reduced-row-echelon-form) has pivots $1$ and zeros elsewhere in each pivot column

Pivot columns: $1,3$; free variables: $x_2,x_4$

The boxed columns are $\vct{e}_1,\vct{e}_2$: the first two columns of $\mat{I}_3$

$$
\operatorname{rank}(\mat{A})=2
$$

::: {.notes}
Subtract twice the first row from the second and the first row from the third
to get $(0,0,-2,-2)$ and $(0,0,1,1)$. Keep the latter as pivot row, eliminate
the former, then subtract the pivot row from the first row. This gives the
displayed reduced matrix. The teal outlines mark whole pivot columns,
including their trailing zero entries. They are the first two columns of I_3;
the same selected columns in the nonzero-row factor R form I_2.
:::

## Column and row bases come from different matrices {#column-and-row-bases-come-from-different-matrices}

For the running $3\times4$ matrix, the pivot columns are $1$ and $3$

A basis for the column space uses pivot columns of the [original]{.alert} matrix:

$$
\left\{
\begin{bmatrix}1\\2\\1\end{bmatrix},
\begin{bmatrix}1\\0\\2\end{bmatrix}
\right\}
$$

A basis for the row space uses nonzero rows of the [reduced]{.alert} matrix:

$$
\left\{
\begin{bmatrix}1\\2\\0\\2\end{bmatrix},
\begin{bmatrix}0\\0\\1\\1\end{bmatrix}
\right\}
$$

::: {.key-point}
Row reduction preserves the row space but generally changes the column space
:::

## Free variables build a basis for the null space {#free-variables-build-a-basis-for-the-null-space}

Row operations preserve solutions: $\mat{A}\vct{x}=\vct{0}\iff\operatorname{rref}(\mat{A})\vct{x}=\vct{0}$

For the running $3\times4$ matrix, the free variables are $x_2,x_4$:

$$
x_1=-2x_2-2x_4,
\qquad
x_3=-x_4
$$

Therefore

$$
\vct{x}
=x_2\begin{bmatrix}-2\\1\\0\\0\end{bmatrix}
+x_4\begin{bmatrix}-2\\0\\-1\\1\end{bmatrix}
$$

and

$$
\dim(\operatorname{Null}(\mat{A}))=2
$$

::: {.key-point}
Each free variable contributes one independent null-space direction
:::

# Rank and Solution Sets

- [Rank-nullity counts inputs](#rank-nullity-counts-inputs)
- [Rank separates existence from uniqueness](#rank-separates-existence-from-uniqueness)
- [Rank-nullity predicts solution sets](#rank-nullity-predicts-solution-sets)

## Rank-nullity counts inputs {#rank-nullity-counts-inputs}

For an $m\times n$ matrix $\mat{A}$,

$$
\operatorname{rank}(\mat{A})
+\operatorname{nullity}(\mat{A})=n
$$

Running $3\times4$ example: two pivots and two free variables

$$
\underbrace{2}_{\text{rank}}+\underbrace{2}_{\text{nullity}}
=\underbrace{4}_{\text{input variables}}
$$

Interpretation:

- rank counts independent input directions that remain visible
- nullity counts independent input directions sent to zero

::: {.key-point}
Rank-nullity accounts for every direction in the input space
:::

---

## Rank separates existence from uniqueness {#rank-separates-existence-from-uniqueness}

For $\mat{A}\in\reals^{m\times n}$ and $\mat{A}\vct{x}=\vct{b}$:

| Question | Condition |
|---|---|
| Does this $\vct{b}$ have a solution? | $\vct{b}\in\operatorname{Col}(\mat{A})$ |
| Is a solution unique, when it exists? | $\operatorname{Null}(\mat{A})=\{\vct{0}\}$, or rank $=n$ |
| Does every $\vct{b}\in\reals^m$ have a solution? | $\operatorname{Col}(\mat{A})=\reals^m$, or rank $=m$ |

Two inputs produce the same output exactly when

$$
\mat{A}\vct{x}=\mat{A}\vct{x}'
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\vct{x}-\vct{x}'\in\operatorname{Null}(\mat{A})
$$

::: {.key-point}
For a square matrix, full rank gives existence and uniqueness for every right-hand side
:::

::: {.notes}
Full column rank gives at most one solution; it does not guarantee existence
for every right-hand side in a taller system. Full row rank guarantees every
right-hand side is attainable; a wider system can still have many solutions.
The square case reconnects these statements to the invertible-matrix results
in Inverses. Whenever a solution x_p exists, all solutions are
x_p + Null(A); choosing a null-space basis supplies the independent parameters.
:::

## Rank-nullity predicts solution sets {#rank-nullity-predicts-solution-sets}

::: {.exitem}
<span class="exbullet">$\exstar$</span>
<span>Compare two $3\times5$ matrices: $\operatorname{rank}(\mat{A})=2$ and $\operatorname{rank}(\mat{B})=3$
<span class="exsub">Find each nullity</span>
<span class="exsub">Could either system $\mat{A}\vct{x}=\vct{b}$ or $\mat{B}\vct{x}=\vct{b}$ have exactly one solution?</span>
<span class="exsub">Which system is solvable for every $\vct{b}\in\reals^3$?</span>
</span>
:::

::: {.notes}
Use $\mat{A}$ on the board and leave $\mat{B}$ for students. The nullities
are $3$ and $2$. Neither system can have exactly one solution when consistent,
because each null space contains nonzero directions. Only $\mat{B}$ has rank
$3$ and hence column space $\reals^3$, so only $\mat{B}\vct{x}=\vct{b}$ is
solvable for every $\vct{b}\in\reals^3$.
:::

# Orthogonal Pairs

- [An orthogonal complement contains all perpendicular directions](#an-orthogonal-complement-contains-all-perpendicular-directions)
- [The four spaces pair through orthogonality](#the-four-spaces-pair-through-orthogonality)
- [Example: see both orthogonal pairs](#worked-example-see-both-orthogonal-pairs)

## An orthogonal complement contains all perpendicular directions {#an-orthogonal-complement-contains-all-perpendicular-directions}

For a subspace $W\subseteq\reals^d$, its [orthogonal complement]{.alert} is

$$
W^\perp=\{\vct{z}\in\reals^d:\vct{z}^{\mathsf T}\vct{w}=0
\text{ for every }\vct{w}\in W\}
$$

It is enough to check the dot product with each vector in a basis of $W$

Every $\vct{x}\in\reals^d$ has a unique decomposition

$$
\vct{x}=\vct{w}+\vct{z},\qquad \vct{w}\in W,\quad \vct{z}\in W^\perp
$$

::: {.key-point}
$\dim(W)+\dim(W^\perp)=d$: the two subspaces account for every direction
:::

::: {.notes}
This is Euclidean orthogonality using the dot product from Euclidean Spaces.
If z is perpendicular to the basis vectors, linearity makes it perpendicular
to every combination. The Euclidean orthogonal-decomposition theorem gives
existence. Uniqueness follows because W intersects W^perp only in zero:
a vector perpendicular to itself has zero squared length.
:::

## The four spaces pair through orthogonality {#the-four-spaces-pair-through-orthogonality}

For $\mat{A}\in\reals^{m\times n}$ with $r=\operatorname{rank}(\mat{A})$,

$$
\operatorname{Row}(\mat{A})^\perp
=\operatorname{Null}(\mat{A})
\qquad\text{inside }\reals^n
$$

$$
\operatorname{Col}(\mat{A})^\perp
=\operatorname{Null}(\mat{A}^{\mathsf T})
\qquad\text{inside }\reals^m
$$

The dimensions balance:

$$
\dim(\operatorname{Row}(\mat{A}))=\dim(\operatorname{Col}(\mat{A}))=r
$$

$$
\dim(\operatorname{Null}(\mat{A}))=n-r,
\qquad
\dim(\operatorname{Null}(\mat{A}^{\mathsf T}))=m-r
$$

---

## Example: see both orthogonal pairs {#worked-example-see-both-orthogonal-pairs}

Take the rank-one matrix

$$
\mat{A}=\begin{bmatrix}1&2&0\\2&4&0\end{bmatrix}
$$

Inside $\reals^3$:

$$
\operatorname{Row}(\mat{A})=\operatorname{span}\{(1,2,0)^{\mathsf T}\},
\qquad
\operatorname{Null}(\mat{A})=\{(-2s,s,t)^{\mathsf T}:s,t\in\reals\}
$$

Their dot product is $-2s+2s=0$

Inside $\reals^2$:

$$
\operatorname{Col}(\mat{A})=\operatorname{span}\{(1,2)^{\mathsf T}\},
\qquad
\operatorname{Null}(\mat{A}^{\mathsf T})=\operatorname{span}\{(-2,1)^{\mathsf T}\}
$$

Their dot product is $-2+2=0$

::: {.key-point}
Row–null orthogonality and column–left-null orthogonality use different
ambient spaces
:::

---

### Orthogonality and ambient spaces {#practice-orthogonality-and-ambient-spaces}

Let

$$
\mat{B}=\begin{bmatrix}1&0&1\\0&1&1\end{bmatrix}
$$

::: {.exitem .lettered}
<span class="exbullet">$\exstar$</span>
<span>Find the two orthogonal pairs
<span class="exsub">Find a basis for $\operatorname{Null}(\mat{B})$; check its dot products with both rows</span>
<span class="exsub">What are $\operatorname{Col}(\mat{B})$ and $\operatorname{Null}(\mat{B}^{\mathsf T})$?</span>
<span class="exsub">Check the dimension sums in $\reals^3$ and $\reals^2$</span>
<span class="exsub">Does it make sense to take the dot product of a row-space vector with a column-space vector here?</span>
</span>
:::

::: {.notes}
The null space has basis {(-1,-1,1)^T}; its dot product with each row is
zero. The column space is R^2 and the left null space is {0}. The dimension
sums are 2+1=3 and 2+0=2. Row-space vectors have three coordinates and
column-space vectors have two, so their dot product is not defined.
:::

# Rank Factorization and the Left Null Space

- [Rank factorization keeps the independent columns and rows](#rank-factorization-keeps-the-independent-columns-and-rows)
- [Check the factorization column by column](#check-the-factorization-column-by-column)
- [Find the left null space](#find-the-left-null-space)

Return to [our running $3\times4$ example](#one-reduction-exposes-the-structure):

$$
\mat{A}=\begin{bmatrix}
1&2&1&3\\
2&4&0&4\\
1&2&2&4
\end{bmatrix}
\quad\longrightarrow\quad
\operatorname{rref}(\mat{A})=\left[
\begin{array}{cccc}
\bbox[3px,border:2px solid teal]{\begin{matrix}1\\0\\0\end{matrix}}
&\begin{matrix}2\\0\\0\end{matrix}
&\bbox[3px,border:2px solid teal]{\begin{matrix}0\\1\\0\end{matrix}}
&\begin{matrix}2\\1\\0\end{matrix}
\end{array}
\right]
$$

The [RREF]({{< meta decks.d01.file >}}#reduced-row-echelon-form) has pivot columns $1$ and $3$

## Rank factorization keeps the independent columns and rows {#rank-factorization-keeps-the-independent-columns-and-rows}

For the running $3\times4$ matrix, take original columns $1,3$ for $\mat{C}$
and the two nonzero RREF rows for $\mat{R}$:

$$
\mat{C}=
\begin{bmatrix}
1&1\\
2&0\\
1&2
\end{bmatrix},
\qquad
\mat{R}=
\left[
\begin{array}{cccc}
\bbox[3px,border:2px solid teal]{\begin{matrix}1\\0\end{matrix}}
&\begin{matrix}2\\0\end{matrix}
&\bbox[3px,border:2px solid teal]{\begin{matrix}0\\1\end{matrix}}
&\begin{matrix}2\\1\end{matrix}
\end{array}
\right]
$$

Row operations preserve column relations; the boxed columns form $\mat{I}_2$,
making $\mat{R}$ the coefficient matrix:

$$
\mat{A}=\mat{C}\mat{R},
\qquad
\operatorname{rref}(\mat{A})=\begin{bmatrix}\mat{R}\\\mat{0}\end{bmatrix}
$$

::: {.key-point}
The columns of $\mat{C}$ form a basis for $\operatorname{Col}(\mat{A})$

The rows of $\mat{R}$ form a basis for $\operatorname{Row}(\mat{A})$
:::

---

### Row operations preserve column relations {#row-operations-preserve-column-relations}

Let $\mat{B}$ be obtained from $\mat{A}\in\reals^{m\times n}$ by reversible row operations

For any coefficient vector $\vct{c}\in\reals^n$, the homogeneous solutions stay the same:

$$
\mat{A}\vct{c}=\vct{0}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\mat{B}\vct{c}=\vct{0}
$$

Write $\vct{A}_j,\vct{B}_j$ for column $j$ of each matrix; matrix–vector multiplication gives

$$
\sum_{j=1}^n c_j\vct{A}_j=\vct{0}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\sum_{j=1}^n c_j\vct{B}_j=\vct{0}
$$

Move any column relation to one side to apply this zero test

::: {.key-point}
Every column relation survives elimination with the same coefficients
:::

::: {.notes}
Each elementary row operation preserves the entire solution set of a
homogeneous system, and its inverse gives the reverse implication. Since
A c is the sum of c_j A_j, the same coefficients c describe exactly the same
zero relations in A and B. In particular, move A_j minus a proposed
combination of selected columns to the left. The corresponding relation is
zero before reduction if and only if it is zero after reduction. This
argument applies even when column j is one of the selected columns.
:::

---

### Why the rank-factorization recipe works {#why-the-rank-factorization-recipe-works}

For $\mat{A}\in\reals^{m\times n}$ of rank $r$, let $\mat{B}=\operatorname{rref}(\mat{A})$

List pivot indices left to right: $p_1<\cdots<p_r$

Use $\mat{C}=[\vct{A}_{p_1}\ \cdots\ \vct{A}_{p_r}]\in\reals^{m\times r}$; collect the nonzero rows in $\mat{R}\in\reals^{r\times n}$

Let $\vct{d}_j\in\reals^r$ be column $j$ of $\mat{R}$; $\mat{B}$ has $m-r$ trailing zero rows

RREF pivot columns have a single $1$, so

$$
\vct{B}_j=\begin{bmatrix}\vct{d}_j\\\vct{0}\end{bmatrix}
=\sum_{\ell=1}^r (\vct{d}_j)_\ell\vct{B}_{p_\ell}
$$

Undo the row operations, preserving those coefficients:

$$
\vct{A}_j=\sum_{\ell=1}^r(\vct{d}_j)_\ell\vct{A}_{p_\ell}
=\mat{C}\vct{d}_j
$$

::: {.key-point}
This holds for every column $j$, so $\mat{A}=\mat{C}\mat{R}$
:::

::: {.notes}
B contains the r nonzero rows of R, followed by m-r zero rows. Its selected
pivot column p_l is [e_l;0], where e_l is the lth standard basis vector in
R^r. Thus any reduced column is the combination of these pivot columns with
coefficients given by its top r entries. The preceding slide proves that
reversing row reduction restores A's columns with those same coefficients.
Collect d_j as the columns of R to obtain A=C R.

C has r independent columns because their reduced versions are independent
unit columns and row reduction preserves dependence relations. The r rows
of R are independent because their pivot-column block is I_r. Row
operations preserve the row space, so those rows span Row(A). Consequently
Col(C)=Col(A), Row(R)=Row(A), and both factors have rank r.

An equivalent matrix proof uses the invertible row-operation product M:
M A=B=rref(A)=[R;0] and M C=[I_r;0]. Then
M(C R)=[I_r;0] R=[R;0]=M A. Multiply by M^{-1}.
For rank zero A is the zero matrix; the empty-column C and empty-row R
give the zero product. If m=r, the displayed bottom zero block is empty.
:::

---

### Echelon form finds bases; RREF supplies these coefficients {#echelon-bases-and-rref-coefficients}

For our running $3\times4$ matrix $\mat{A}$, an echelon form with unit pivots is

$$
\mat{E}=\begin{bmatrix}
1&2&1&3\\
0&0&1&1\\
0&0&0&0
\end{bmatrix}
\xrightarrow{R_1\leftarrow R_1-R_2}
\operatorname{rref}(\mat{A})=\left[
\begin{array}{cccc}
\bbox[3px,border:2px solid teal]{\begin{matrix}1\\0\\0\end{matrix}}
&\begin{matrix}2\\0\\0\end{matrix}
&\bbox[3px,border:2px solid teal]{\begin{matrix}0\\1\\0\end{matrix}}
&\begin{matrix}2\\1\\0\end{matrix}
\end{array}
\right]
$$

- Either form identifies original columns $1,3$ as a column-space basis
- The nonzero rows of either form give a row-space basis
- Remove the zero row from the boxed pivot columns to obtain $\mat{I}_2$ in $\mat{R}$

::: {.key-point}
For the direct formula $\mat{A}=\mat{C}\mat{R}$, use the nonzero RREF rows
:::

::: {.notes}
Echelon form is enough for both pivot-column extraction and a nonzero-row
basis. Back substitution also finds null-space bases. RREF is not necessary
for the existence of rank factorization. It is necessary for the particular
shortcut used here: choose C as the original pivot columns and take R
directly from the reduced rows. E's pivot columns in its first two rows form
the matrix [[1,1],[0,1]], whereas R's form I_2. Thus the nonzero rows E_r
are not the coefficient matrix for these selected original columns. One can
instead use E_p^{-1} E_r, where E_p is that invertible pivot-column block;
clearing above the pivots performs exactly that normalization here.
:::

---

## Check the factorization column by column {#check-the-factorization-column-by-column}

Recall the independent columns and their coefficient matrix:

$$
\mat{C}=[\vct{C}_1\ \vct{C}_2]
=\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\2&0\\1&2\end{bmatrix},
\qquad
\mat{R}=\left[
\begin{array}{cccc}
\bbox[3px,border:2px solid teal]{\begin{matrix}1\\0\end{matrix}}
&\begin{matrix}2\\0\end{matrix}
&\bbox[3px,border:2px solid teal]{\begin{matrix}0\\1\end{matrix}}
&\begin{matrix}2\\1\end{matrix}
\end{array}
\right]
$$

The columns of $\mat{R}$ give the coefficients, just as in
[the matrix product by columns in {{< meta decks.d01.short_title >}}]({{< meta decks.d01.file >}}#matrix-matrix-multiplication-collects-dot-products):

$$
\begin{aligned}
\vct{A}_1&=\vct{C}_1 &
\vct{A}_2&=2\vct{C}_1\\
\vct{A}_3&=\vct{C}_2 &
\vct{A}_4&=2\vct{C}_1+\vct{C}_2
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus $\mat{C}\mat{R}$ rebuilds all four columns of $\mat{A}$

::: {.key-point}
For the ordered column-space basis $\mathcal{C}=(\vct{C}_1,\vct{C}_2)$,

$$
[\mat{A}\vct{x}]_{\mathcal{C}}=\mat{R}\vct{x}
$$

$\mat{R}\vct{x}$ gives the coordinates; $\mat{C}$ rebuilds the output
:::

---

### Construct rank factorizations {#practice-constructing-rank-factorizations}

::: {.exitem .lettered}
<span class="exbullet">$\exstar$</span>
<span>For each matrix $\mat{M}$ below, find $\mat{C}$ and $\mat{R}$ with $\mat{M}=\mat{C}\mat{R}$
<span class="exsub">$\displaystyle\mat{B}=\begin{bmatrix}1&2&0\\0&0&1\\1&2&1\end{bmatrix}$</span>
<span class="exsub">$\displaystyle\mat{D}=\begin{bmatrix}1&0&2&3\\2&1&4&7\end{bmatrix}$</span>
</span>
:::

For each factorization, identify bases for the row and column spaces

::: {.notes}
For $\mat{B}$, use columns $1$ and $3$:
$\mat{C}=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\0&1\\1&1\end{bmatrix}$ and
$\mat{R}=\begin{bmatrix}1&2&0\\0&0&1\end{bmatrix}$.
For $\mat{D}$, use columns $1$ and $2$:
$\mat{C}=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\2&1\end{bmatrix}$ and
$\mat{R}=\begin{bmatrix}1&0&2&3\\0&1&0&1\end{bmatrix}$.
The columns of each $\mat{C}$ and rows of each $\mat{R}$ give the requested
bases.
:::

## Find the left null space {#find-the-left-null-space}

For the running $3\times4$ matrix, the column-space basis is stored in

$$
\mat{C}=\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\2&0\\1&2\end{bmatrix}
$$

Every column of $\mat{A}$ is a combination of these two columns

Thus $\mat{A}^{\mathsf T}\vct{y}=\vct{0}\iff\mat{C}^{\mathsf T}\vct{y}=\vct{0}$:

$$
y_1+2y_2+y_3=0,
\qquad y_1+2y_3=0
$$

Taking $y_3=2$ gives $\vct{y}=(-4,1,2)^{\mathsf T}$

$$
\operatorname{Null}(\mat{A}^{\mathsf T})
=\operatorname{span}\{(-4,1,2)^{\mathsf T}\}
$$

This vector is perpendicular to both columns of $\mat{C}$

---

### Left-null vectors test compatibility of equations {#left-null-vectors-test-compatibility-of-equations}

If $\mat{A}^{\mathsf T}\vct{y}=\vct{0}$ and $\mat{A}\vct{x}=\vct{b}$, then

$$
\vct{y}^{\mathsf T}\vct{b}
=\vct{y}^{\mathsf T}\mat{A}\vct{x}=0
$$

A right-hand side is attainable exactly when it is perpendicular to every
left-null vector

In our example, $\operatorname{Null}(\mat{A}^{\mathsf T})$ has basis
$\{(-4,1,2)^{\mathsf T}\}$, so consistency is equivalent to

$$
-4b_1+b_2+2b_3=0
$$

::: {.exitem}
<span class="exbullet">$\exstar$</span>
<span>Use this test for $\vct{b}=(0,1,0)^{\mathsf T}$ and $\vct{b}=(1,2,1)^{\mathsf T}$</span>
:::

::: {.notes}
For (0,1,0)^T, y^T b=1, so there is no solution. For (1,2,1)^T, the
condition holds, and b is the first column of A, so x=(1,0,0,0)^T solves it.
The sufficiency comes from Col(A)=Null(A^T)^perp. The same y also describes a
linear dependence among the equations; a consistent right-hand side must
obey that relation. This is a concrete solvability certificate, not just
another dimension count.
:::

---

### One matrix supports several basis questions {#one-matrix-supports-several-basis-questions}

Return to [the rank-factorization exercise](#practice-constructing-rank-factorizations):

$$
\mat{B}=\begin{bmatrix}1&2&0\\0&0&1\\1&2&1\end{bmatrix},
\qquad
\mat{C}=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\0&1\\1&1\end{bmatrix}
\quad\text{(original columns $1,3$)}
$$

::: {.exitem}
<span class="exbullet">$\exstar$</span>
<span>Complete the picture of its four fundamental subspaces
<span class="exsub">Find bases for $\operatorname{Null}(\mat{B})$ and $\operatorname{Null}(\mat{B}^{\mathsf T})$</span>
<span class="exsub">Check that your left-null vector is perpendicular to both columns of $\mat{C}$</span>
<span class="exsub">Compare the four dimensions with rank–nullity</span>
</span>
:::

::: {.notes}
For $\mat{B}$, a null-space basis is $\{(-2,1,0)^{\mathsf T}\}$, and a
left-null basis is $\{(-1,-1,1)^{\mathsf T}\}$. Each is orthogonal to the
appropriate row or column basis. The dimensions are $2,1,2,1$ for column,
null, row, and left null, respectively.
:::

# What the Structure Buys Us

Preview: Anton §§8.1 and 8.4

- [A basis turns an abstract problem into a matrix problem](#a-basis-turns-an-abstract-problem-into-a-matrix-problem)
- [Example: differentiation is a matrix](#worked-example-differentiation-is-a-matrix)
- [A well-chosen basis can simplify an operator](#a-well-chosen-basis-can-simplify-an-operator)

## A basis turns an abstract problem into a matrix problem {#a-basis-turns-an-abstract-problem-into-a-matrix-problem}

Let $V$ and $W$ be finite-dimensional real vector spaces

A [linear transformation]{.alert} $T:V\to W$ preserves linear combinations:

$$
T(c\vct{u}+d\vct{v})=cT(\vct{u})+dT(\vct{v})
$$

Choose ordered bases $\mathcal{B}=(\vct{b}_1,\ldots,\vct{b}_n)$ for the input $V$
and $\mathcal{C}$ for the output $W$: $\dim(V)=n$, $\dim(W)=m$

Recall [coordinates]({{< meta decks.d06b.file >}}#a-basis-gives-every-vector-unique-coordinates): $[\vct{v}]_{\mathcal{B}}=(c_1,\ldots,c_n)^{\mathsf T}$ means $\vct{v}=\sum_{j=1}^n c_j\vct{b}_j$

The $m\times n$ coordinate matrix $\mat{M}$ has column $j$ equal to $[T(\vct{b}_j)]_{\mathcal{C}}$
and satisfies

$$
[T(\vct{v})]_{\mathcal{C}}
=\mat{M}[\vct{v}]_{\mathcal{B}}
$$

::: {.key-point}
A linear transformation is determined by its action on a basis
:::

---

## Example: differentiation is a matrix {#worked-example-differentiation-is-a-matrix}

Let $D:\mathbb{P}_2\to\mathbb{P}_1$ send $p$ to $p'$

Use $\mathcal{B}=(1,t,t^2)$ for the input and $\mathcal{C}=(1,t)$ for the output

$$
D(1)=0,
\qquad D(t)=1,
\qquad D(t^2)=2t
$$

Their output coordinate vectors become the columns:

$$
\mat{M}=\begin{bmatrix}0&1&0\\0&0&2\end{bmatrix},
\qquad [D(p)]_{\mathcal{C}}=\mat{M}[p]_{\mathcal{B}}
$$

For $p=2-3t+5t^2$,

$$
\mat{M}\begin{bmatrix}2\\-3\\5\end{bmatrix}
=\begin{bmatrix}-3\\10\end{bmatrix}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad p'=-3+10t
$$

::: {.key-point}
Apply the map to each input basis vector; put its output coordinates in a column
:::

---

### Evaluate a polynomial with a matrix {#practice-evaluate-a-polynomial-with-a-matrix}

Let $T:\mathbb{P}_2\to\reals^2$ be

$$
T(p)=\begin{bmatrix}p(0)\\p(1)\end{bmatrix}
$$

Use $\mathcal{B}=(1,t,t^2)$ and standard output coordinates

::: {.exitem .lettered}
<span class="exbullet">$\exstar$</span>
<span>Construct and interpret the matrix of $T$
<span class="exsub">Find $T(1)$, $T(t)$, and $T(t^2)$; make them the columns of $\mat{M}$</span>
<span class="exsub">Use $\mat{M}$ to evaluate $p=2-3t+5t^2$ at both points</span>
<span class="exsub">Find a nonzero polynomial sent to zero; explain why two values cannot identify every quadratic</span>
</span>
:::

::: {.notes}
The columns are (1,1)^T, (0,1)^T, (0,1)^T, so M=[[1,0,0],[1,1,1]].
For p=2-3t+5t^2, the output is (2,4)^T. Its null space consists of coefficient
vectors (0,-s,s)^T: the corresponding polynomials are s(t^2-t).
The rank is two and nullity one. Adding any multiple of t^2-t leaves both
sampled values unchanged. T preserves linear combinations by pointwise
evaluation.
:::


## A well-chosen basis can simplify an operator {#a-well-chosen-basis-can-simplify-an-operator}

For $\mat{A}:\reals^n\to\reals^n$, use the same basis for input and output

For a basis $\mathcal{B}=(\vct{b}_1,\ldots,\vct{b}_n)$ of $\reals^n$,

$$
\mat{P}=[\vct{b}_1\ \cdots\ \vct{b}_n],
\qquad \vct{x}=\mat{P}[\vct{x}]_{\mathcal{B}}
$$

The matrix in $\mathcal{B}$ coordinates is $\mat{P}^{-1}\mat{A}\mat{P}$

[{{< meta decks.d07.short_title >}}]({{< meta decks.d07.file >}}) asks whether a basis can make it diagonal:

$$
\mat{P}^{-1}\mat{A}\mat{P}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
\lambda_1&&0\\
&\ddots&\\
0&&\lambda_n
\end{bmatrix}
$$

Each basis vector must satisfy $\mat{A}\vct{b}_j=\lambda_j\vct{b}_j$: its span is preserved

::: {.key-point}
Eigenvectors are basis candidates adapted to the action of a matrix
:::

# Big Ideas {data-state="goldborder"}

- Reduction reveals bases for row, column, and null spaces
- Rank separates attainable outputs from lost input directions
- Row/null and column/left-null spaces form orthogonal pairs
- Rank factorization separates independent columns from their combinations
- Left-null vectors give compatibility conditions for the equations
- Bases turn finite-dimensional linear maps into matrices

::: {.key-point}
$\mat{A}\vct{x}=\vct{b}$ is solvable iff $\vct{b}\in\operatorname{Col}(\mat{A})$, equivalently $\vct{y}^{\mathsf T}\vct{b}=0$ for every $\vct{y}\in\operatorname{Null}(\mat{A}^{\mathsf T})$

Choose $\vct{x}_p$ with $\mat{A}\vct{x}_p=\vct{b}$; columns of $\mat{N}$ form a basis of $\operatorname{Null}(\mat{A})$

$$
\text{All solutions:}\quad
\vct{x}=\vct{x}_p+\mat{N}\vct{t},\qquad \vct{t}\in\reals^{n-r}
$$
:::

::: {.notes}
This is a cumulative synthesis, rather than a chronology of deck titles.
Retain the original question Ax=b, the reversible computations and reusable
factors, the geometric meaning of actions, and the progressively richer
descriptions of vectors. N's columns are a basis of Null(A), so t supplies
exactly n-r independent free parameters. A column-space basis C describes
which right-hand sides are attainable; a null-space basis N describes all
inputs that give the same attainable right-hand side. The condition can
also be tested by y^T b=0 for every left-null vector y. Full row rank r=m
makes every b attainable, and full column rank r=n gives uniqueness when a
solution exists. Projections, point differences, and cross-product normals
and areas retain the Euclidean geometric tools from the earlier deck.
:::
